title: Junebug Creek Rising Again
premise: Jonah Reyes, a marine biologist hiding in a coastal research station after a decade-old betrayal destroyed her family's name, is assigned an anonymous pen-pal through a prison literacy program—only to discover her correspondent is Caleb Marsh, the man whose testimony sent her father to prison and who has just been released on new evidence of his own wrongful conviction. As their letters deepen into something neither can name, Jonah must decide whether the truth she rehearsed for ten years—that she saw what really happened that night at Junebug Creek—is worth finally speaking aloud. When Caleb's appeal hearing arrives with only days left before evidence disappears forever, Jonah testifies, freeing them both from the past; the book ends with the two of them releasing rehabilitated sea turtles together, choosing each other not as enemies or strangers but as the people their honesty made.
about_author: Marguerite Brightwater is the pen name of a former Gulf Coast journalist who covered small-town courtrooms for fifteen years before turning to fiction. She writes romances about people who find love on the far side of hard truths, and she still keeps a battered notebook of overheard sentences from courthouse steps.

chapters.title: Counting Turtles
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Five years into her careful, invisible life at Junebug Creek Research Station, Jonah counts nesting loggerheads and avoids the town that remembers her family's disgrace. Her supervisor signs the station up for a prison pen-pal program without asking her. Emotional beat: the ache of safety that feels like suffocation.

chapters.title: The Assignment
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The program coordinator assigns her prisoner #4471 anonymously, standard protocol. Jonah writes a stiff first letter about tides and turtle nests, telling herself it means nothing. A storm knocks out the station's internet, making letters her only outside contact. Emotional beat: reluctant curiosity cracking open routine.

chapters.title: Inmate 4471
chapters.summary: Caleb's POV. In his final weeks at Alligator Point Correctional, Caleb receives a letter full of tide charts and dry humor. He answers honestly about the books he's read and the years he lost. He doesn't tell her he's being released next month under a vacated conviction. Emotional beat: cautious hope he doesn't trust.

chapters.title: Letters Like Weather
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Over six weeks, letters trade between them: her observations of the creek, his memories of growing up three miles downstream. They argue about Faulkner, laugh about a raccoon raiding the station. Neither uses real names. Emotional beat: intimacy built entirely on words.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At the hardware store, Jonah overhears that Caleb Marsh—the man whose testimony convicted her father—is getting out. Panic floods back: the trial, her mother's collapse, the sentence she rehearsed and never said. She almost burns the letters. Emotional beat: terror that the past has found her address.

chapters.title: The Last Letter Before Freedom
chapters.summary: Caleb's POV. Caleb confesses in writing that he's being released, that he took a plea-adjacent testimony at nineteen because someone threatened him, and that he's spent eleven years trying to undo it. He asks his pen-pal, whoever she is, whether a person can be forgiven for a lie told out of fear. Emotional beat: raw vulnerability.

chapters.title: Release Day
chapters.summary: Caleb's POV. Caleb walks out to a bus stop, a duffel bag, and a town that spits at ex-cons. He takes a job shucking oysters and starts pulling records for his exoneration hearing—thirty days away. He writes one more letter he never mails. Emotional beat: freedom that feels like falling.

chapters.title: Recognition
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Sorting returned mail at the post office, Jonah sees Caleb's handwriting on an unmailed letter and recognizes it instantly from the trial exhibits she memorized as a teenager. Her pen-pal is him. Her enemy knows her voice but not her face. Emotional beat: vertigo—every tender word now doubles as betrayal.

chapters.title: The Rehearsed Sentence
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Flashback chapter: sixteen-year-old Jonah at Junebug Creek the night of the accident, seeing what actually happened, being coached by her frightened parents into silence. The sentence she never testified to has lived in her throat for a decade. Emotional beat: understanding how silence calcified into identity.

chapters.title: Answering Anyway
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Despite everything, Jonah writes back—testing him, probing whether his remorse is real or performed. His reply is unflinching about his own cowardice. She begins visiting the county archive at night, pulling the case file. Emotional beat: hatred and longing becoming indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Oyster House
chapters.summary: Caleb's POV. Caleb spots Jonah at the oyster house where he works and realizes his pen-pal's tide-chart details match the woman everyone calls the Reyes girl. He says nothing, terrified of losing the one honest relationship he has. They share a shift, charged and wordless. Emotional beat: proximity without permission.

chapters.title: The Creek at Night
chapters.summary: Both POVs. A stranded hatchling rescue brings them to the same stretch of creek after dark. Working side by side by flashlight, they talk around the truth until Caleb says her name. The recognition detonates quietly between them. Emotional beat: the moment anonymity dies and everything becomes personal.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Station
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah confronts Caleb: you let me fall for you while knowing who I was. He counters that she did the same. Both are right. He shows her the evidence he's gathered—a witness statement proving the crash was caused by the town's beloved former sheriff. Emotional beat: anger transmuting into alliance.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Shadow
chapters.summary: Caleb's POV. Caleb explains the threat that made him lie at nineteen: the sheriff owned his family's debt. Now the sheriff's protégé runs the county, and the missing evidence sits in an old evidence locker scheduled for destruction the week after Caleb's hearing. Emotional beat: the clock starting to tick audibly.

chapters.title: Allies in the Dark
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Jonah and Caleb break into the archived records room together, finding the sheriff's dashcam tape misfiled for a decade. Nearly caught by a night deputy, they escape with copies. In the truck afterward, shaking, they hold hands for the first time. Emotional beat: trust forged in shared risk.

chapters.title: Her Father's Doorstep
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah visits her father, newly paroled himself, and tells him she intends to testify. He begs her to stay silent—the town, the shame, the futility. For the first time she refuses him, saying the rehearsed sentence aloud in his kitchen. Emotional beat: breaking the family inheritance of silence.

chapters.title: The Threat
chapters.summary: Caleb's POV. Someone torches Caleb's rented room; the tape copy survives only because Jonah kept a second set. A warning note names Jonah. Caleb realizes testifying will paint a target on her, and offers to withdraw so she won't pay his price. She refuses to be protected out of her own story. Emotional beat: love expressed as refusal.

chapters.title: Twenty-Nine Days
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. With the hearing moved up and the original tape scheduled for destruction, Jonah files an affidavit and petitions to testify despite the DA's stonewalling. The town turns hostile; her job is threatened. Caleb and Jonah work nights preparing her, and the letters continue—now signed with real names. Emotional beat: fear metabolized into resolve.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Both POVs. In a packed courtroom, Caleb testifies to the coercion he endured; then Jonah takes the stand and delivers the sentence she rehearsed for ten years, describing exactly what she saw the night of the crash. The misfiled tape corroborates her. The judge orders the conviction vacated and opens an investigation into the former sheriff. Emotional beat: catharsis—the truth spoken at last, costing everything and freeing more.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The town splits between vindication and fury; the station director, revealed to have quietly supported her all along, defends her job. Her father calls, unable to apologize fully, and Jonah accepts that some reconciliations stay partial. Caleb, legally free, prepares to leave town to give her space. Emotional beat: grief and relief tangled together.

chapters.title: The Letter That Was Never Mailed
chapters.summary: Caleb's POV. At the bus depot, Jonah finds him—not with arguments but with his own unsent letter, the one he wrote in week seven, which she intercepted weeks ago and now returns annotated in her handwriting: yes, a person can be forgiven; she already had. Emotional beat: the romance resolving through the medium that built it.

chapters.title: Junebug Creek Rising
chapters.summary: Both POVs, closing scene. One year later: the creek's record turtle season, Caleb working at the station, their letters framed above the desk though they live three miles apart no longer. They release the season's last hatchlings into the surf and watch them go. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace—two people who chose truth and found each other on the other side.
